Parent assembly (the supplied Steps 1-5, specialised). Assume n >= 1, p > n, U open, AllardHypotheses H p delta rho, y in spt V with |y| < rho, and epsilon > 0. Put mu := V.weight and omega := omega_n > 0 (pi^(n/2) > 0 and Gamma(n/2 + 1) > 0).
1. y lies in spt mu, because spt V = U ∩ spt mu. Put d := rho - |y| > 0 and r := d/8.
2. (F2) B_(2r)(y) is compact and lies in B_rho(0) ⊆ U, so mu(B_(2r)(y)) < infinity (withDensity_apply, Measure.restrict_restrict, V.integrableOn_mult, Integrable.lintegral_lt_top).
3. (A) K(0, rho) <= ofReal(delta) < infinity. With rho^(p-n) > 0 and 1/p > 0 this gives integral_(B_rho(0)) |H|^p dmu < infinity (ENNReal.rpow_lt_top_iff_of_pos, ENNReal.mul_lt_top_iff).
4. Step 1 constants: kappa := (p-n)/(4p) > 0 and Lambda := max(delta,0)/kappa + 1 > 0, so delta <= kappa Lambda. A := e^(Lambda/2)/2 * Lambda >= 0, beta := 1 - n/p > 0, and c(t) := A (t/r)^beta, so c >= 0 and c(t) -> 0 as t -> 0+.
5. Step 4: for mu-a.e. x, V.HasDensity x theta(x) (ted_tangent_plane_facts (3)) and theta(x) >= 1 (AllardHypotheses).
6. Step 2 at such an x with |x - y| < r.
   - B_(2r)(x) ⊆ B_rho(0) ⊆ U, since |z| <= 2r + r + |y| < rho.
   - integral_(B_(2r)(x)) |H|^p <= integral_(B_rho(0)) |H|^p < infinity.
   - (K-mono) K(x, r) <= K(0, rho) <= delta <= kappa Lambda.
   - So ted_lp_monotonicity applies at (x, R = r, S = 2r, Lambda). It gives F with |F(t) - 1| <= A (t/r)^beta for t in (0, r] (its third bound), and the monotonicity of Phi_x on (0, r] (verbatim hypothesis (b) of child 1).
   - Child 1 with theta_0 = theta(x) gives omega theta(x) <= (1 + c(t)) m_x(t)/t^n + c(t) for t in (0, r]. Also omega <= omega theta(x).
7. Steps 3 and 5: child 2 with (mu, y, omega, r, c) gives exactly the frozen conclusion.

Differences from the literal supplied proof. The first two are specialisations. The third is the equivalent pointwise (contrapositive) form of Step 5. No new mathematics is introduced.
- One uniform radius R = r = d(y)/8, S = 2r is used for all x in B°_r(y), instead of R_z = d(z)/4 and S_z = d(z)/2. The supplied Step 3 already passes to the uniform r_1 = d(z)/8 through c(t/R_(z')) <= c(t/r_1); the sibling theorem is simply applied at the smaller radii.
- Theta is only evaluated at mu-a.e. points, where it exists and equals theta by Step 4. So neither the everywhere-existence part of Step 2 nor Theta as a function is needed.
- Step 5's "the open mu-null set {Theta < 1} ∩ W misses spt mu" is used in the equivalent pointwise form inside child 2. A good point x near y satisfies omega <= omega Theta(x) <= (1 + c) t^(-n) mu(B_(t+eta)(y)) + c, which is the Step 3 chain with z' = x and z = y.

subproblems.title: Monotone corrected mass ratio dominates omega times the density (Simon Ch. 4, 3.9-3.10, 4.5-4.9)
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, mu a measure on R^(n+l), x in R^(n+l), and omega, R, A, beta, theta_0 real numbers with omega > 0, R > 0, beta > 0 and theta_0 >= 0; let F : R -> R. Write B_s(x) for the closed ball and m(s) := toReal(mu(B_s(x))) (toReal(infinity) = 0). Assume (a) |F(t) - 1| <= A (t/R)^beta for all t in (0, R] (real power rpow); (b) F(s)(m(s)/s^n) + (F(s) - 1) <= F(t)(m(t)/t^n) + (F(t) - 1) whenever 0 < s <= t <= R (natural power s^n); (c) mu(B_r(x)) / ofReal(omega r^n) -> ofReal(theta_0) in [0, infinity] as r -> 0+. Then for every t in (0, R]: omega theta_0 <= (1 + A (t/R)^beta)(m(t)/t^n) + A (t/R)^beta.

Source: Steps 2-4 of the parent proof of ted_density_ge_one (Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 4, 3.9-3.10 and 4.5-4.9; the identification of the limit with the multiplicity is Step 4, via Ch. 3, Remark 1.8(2)). There, Step 2 shows that the monotone quantity Phi_z(t) = F_z(t) t^(-n) mu(B_t(z)) + F_z(t) - 1 has a limit l_z as t -> 0+ with l_z <= Phi_z(t), Step 3 uses |F - 1| <= c to get "omega_n Theta(z') = l_(z') <= Phi_(z')(t) <= (1 + c) t^(-n) mu(B_t(z')) + c", and Step 4 identifies the limit with omega_n theta(x) at points where V.HasDensity x (theta x) holds. This child isolates that chain at a single point at which the density is already known to exist. The correction factor F, the monotonicity of Phi and the density are abstract hypotheses, so the statement holds for an arbitrary measure mu.

Notation.
- B_s(x) := closedBall x s (closed ball).
- m(s) := toReal(mu(B_s(x))) for s in R, with toReal(infinity) = 0; so m(s) >= 0 always.
- c(s) := A (s/R)^beta, the real power (rpow); s^n is the natural power.
- Phi(s) := F(s) (m(s)/s^n) + (F(s) - 1).

Hypotheses: omega > 0, R > 0, beta > 0, theta_0 >= 0, and
 (a) |F(t) - 1| <= c(t) for all t in (0, R];
 (b) Phi(s) <= Phi(t) whenever 0 < s <= t <= R;
 (c) mu(B_r(x)) / ofReal(omega r^n) -> ofReal(theta_0) in [0, infinity] as r -> 0+.
No sign condition on A and no finiteness of mu(B_R(x)) is assumed or needed.

Fix t with 0 < t <= R. We prove omega theta_0 <= (1 + c(t)) (m(t)/t^n) + c(t).

1. c(s) -> 0 as s -> 0+. The map s -> s/R is continuous with value 0 at s = 0. Since beta > 0, u -> u^beta is continuous at u = 0 (Filter.Tendsto.rpow_const, side condition 0 <= beta) and 0^beta = 0 (Real.zero_rpow, beta /= 0). Hence c(s) = A (s/R)^beta -> A * 0 = 0 as s -> 0, and therefore also along the right-neighbourhood filter s -> 0+.

2. F(s) -> 1 as s -> 0+. The interval (0, t) is a right-neighbourhood of 0, and every s in (0, t) satisfies 0 < s <= R, so (a) gives 0 <= |F(s) - 1| <= c(s). By step 1 and the squeeze theorem (squeeze_zero'), |F(s) - 1| -> 0, i.e. F(s) -> 1 as s -> 0+.

3. m(s)/s^n -> omega theta_0 as s -> 0+.
 (i) For s in (0, t) put D(s) := ofReal(omega s^n). Since omega s^n > 0, D(s) is finite and toReal(D(s)) = omega s^n.
 (ii) For all Y, D in [0, infinity], toReal(Y/D) = toReal(Y)/toReal(D) (ENNReal.toReal_div; for Y = infinity both sides are 0 when D is finite). Hence, for s in (0, t), omega * toReal(mu(B_s(x)) / D(s)) = omega * m(s)/(omega s^n) = m(s)/s^n.
 (iii) By (c), mu(B_s(x))/D(s) -> ofReal(theta_0), which is a finite point of [0, infinity], and toReal is continuous at finite points (ENNReal.tendsto_toReal). Hence toReal(mu(B_s(x))/D(s)) -> toReal(ofReal(theta_0)) = theta_0, using theta_0 >= 0.
 (iv) Multiplying by the constant omega and using the identity (ii) on the right-neighbourhood (0, t) of 0 gives m(s)/s^n -> omega theta_0 as s -> 0+.

4. Phi(s) -> omega theta_0 as s -> 0+. By steps 2 and 3 and the limit rules for products, sums and differences, Phi(s) = F(s)(m(s)/s^n) + (F(s) - 1) -> 1 * (omega theta_0) + (1 - 1) = omega theta_0.

5. omega theta_0 <= Phi(t). For every s in (0, t) we have 0 < s <= t <= R, hence Phi(s) <= Phi(t) by (b). The interval (0, t) belongs to the right-neighbourhood filter of 0, which is a non-trivial filter on R. Letting s -> 0+ and using step 4 (le_of_tendsto) gives omega theta_0 <= Phi(t).

6. Upper bound for Phi(t). By (a) at this t, F(t) - 1 <= |F(t) - 1| <= c(t), so F(t) <= 1 + c(t). Since m(t) >= 0 and t^n > 0, the ratio m(t)/t^n is >= 0, hence F(t)(m(t)/t^n) <= (1 + c(t))(m(t)/t^n). Adding F(t) - 1 <= c(t) gives Phi(t) <= (1 + c(t))(m(t)/t^n) + c(t).

7. Conclusion. Steps 5 and 6 give omega theta_0 <= (1 + A (t/R)^beta)(toReal(mu(B_t(x)))/t^n) + A (t/R)^beta. Since t in (0, R] was arbitrary, the claim holds for every t in (0, R].

There F is the function given by ted_lp_monotonicity at (x, r, 2r, Lambda): its third bound is (a), its monotonicity conclusion is (b) verbatim, and (c) is V.HasDensity x (theta x) from ted_tangent_plane_facts (3).

subproblems.title: Uniform a.e. density estimate near a support point gives the lower density bound (Simon Ch. 4, 3.11 and Remark 4.10(1))
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, mu a measure on R^(n+l), and y in spt mu (Measure.support: every neighbourhood of y has positive mu-measure). Let omega > 0 and r > 0, and let c : R -> R satisfy c(t) >= 0 for t in (0, r] and c(t) -> 0 as t -> 0+. Assume mu(B_(2r)(y)) < infinity, and that for mu-a.e. x, if |x - y| < r then omega <= (1 + c(t)) (toReal(mu(B_t(x)))/t^n) + c(t) for every t in (0, r] (B denotes closed balls). Then for every epsilon > 0 there is s_0 > 0 with ofReal((1 - epsilon)(omega s^n)) <= mu(B_s(y)) for all s in (0, s_0), i.e. eventually along s -> 0+ (the filter 𝓝[>] 0).

subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Steps 3 and 5 of the parent proof of ted_density_ge_one (Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 4, 3.11 and Remark 4.10(1)). Step 3 proves the upper-semicontinuity estimate through the inclusion B_t(z') ⊆ B_(t+eta)(z), followed by eta -> 0+ (continuity of mu from above on closed balls of finite measure) and then t -> 0+. Step 5 uses that an open mu-null set cannot meet spt mu. Here the two are combined in an equivalent pointwise form: every neighbourhood of a point of spt mu has positive measure, so it contains a point at which the a.e. estimate holds, and the estimate at such points transfers to y through the ball inclusion. The statement is for an arbitrary measure mu.

Notation.
- B_u(z) := closedBall z u (closed) and B°_u(z) := ball z u (open).
- M(u) := toReal(mu(B_u(y))), so M(u) >= 0.
- For x in R^(n+l), P(x) is the statement: if |x - y| < r, then omega <= (1 + c(t)) (toReal(mu(B_t(x)))/t^n) + c(t) for every t in (0, r].
- N := {x : P(x) fails}. The a.e. hypothesis says exactly mu(N) = 0 (ae_iff), as an outer-measure statement; no measurability of N is needed.

Other hypotheses: omega > 0, r > 0, y in spt mu, mu(B_(2r)(y)) < infinity, c(t) >= 0 for t in (0, r], and c(t) -> 0 as t -> 0+.

1. Finite masses near y. For u <= 2r, B_u(y) ⊆ B_(2r)(y). So mu(B_u(y)) <= mu(B_(2r)(y)) < infinity and mu(B_u(y)) = ofReal(M(u)).

2. Good points arbitrarily close to y. Let 0 < eta < r.
   - Since y is in spt mu, every neighbourhood of y has positive mu-measure (Measure.mem_support_iff_forall). B°_eta(y) is such a neighbourhood, so mu(B°_eta(y)) > 0.
   - If B°_eta(y) were contained in N, then mu(B°_eta(y)) <= mu(N) = 0 (measure_mono_null), a contradiction.
   - Hence there is x with |x - y| < eta and P(x). As eta < r, also |x - y| < r, so omega <= (1 + c(t)) (toReal(mu(B_t(x)))/t^n) + c(t) for every t in (0, r].

3. Comparison of balls. Fix t in (0, r] and u in (t, t + r). Put eta := u - t, so 0 < eta < r, and choose x as in step 2.
   - If |z - x| <= t, then |z - y| <= |z - x| + |x - y| < t + eta = u. So B_t(x) ⊆ B_u(y).
   - Since u < t + r <= 2r, step 1 gives mu(B_t(x)) <= mu(B_u(y)) < infinity. Hence toReal(mu(B_t(x))) <= M(u).
   - Because c(t) >= 0 we have 1 + c(t) > 0, and t^n > 0. So step 2 yields
     omega <= (1 + c(t)) (M(u)/t^n) + c(t) for every u in (t, t + r).

4. Letting u decrease to t.
   - The closed balls B_u(y), u > t, are measurable and increase with u. Their intersection over all u > t is B_t(y) (Metric.biInter_gt_closedBall). Moreover 2r > t and mu(B_(2r)(y)) < infinity.
   - By continuity of measure from above along u -> t+ (tendsto_measure_biInter_gt), mu(B_u(y)) -> mu(B_t(y)).
   - Since mu(B_t(y)) < infinity (step 1) and toReal is continuous at finite points (ENNReal.tendsto_toReal), M(u) -> M(t). Hence (1 + c(t)) (M(u)/t^n) + c(t) -> (1 + c(t)) (M(t)/t^n) + c(t) as u -> t+.
   - The inequality of step 3 holds on the right-neighbourhood (t, t + r) of t. The right-neighbourhood filter of t is a non-trivial filter on R. Passing to the limit u -> t+ (ge_of_tendsto) gives
     (*) omega <= (1 + c(t)) (M(t)/t^n) + c(t) for every t in (0, r].

5. Case epsilon >= 1. For every s > 0, (1 - epsilon)(omega s^n) <= 0, so ofReal((1 - epsilon)(omega s^n)) = 0 <= mu(B_s(y)). Thus the inequality holds for all s > 0, in particular eventually as s -> 0+.

6. Case 0 < epsilon < 1.
   (i) Put gamma := epsilon omega / (1 + omega) > 0, so gamma (1 + omega) = epsilon omega.
   (ii) Since c(s) -> 0 as s -> 0+ and (0, r) is a right-neighbourhood of 0, eventually as s -> 0+ we have both c(s) < gamma and s in (0, r).
   (iii) Fix such an s and put q := M(s)/s^n >= 0. By (*) with t = s, q >= 0 and 0 <= c(s) < gamma,
     omega <= (1 + c(s)) q + c(s) <= (1 + gamma) q + gamma.
   (iv) Suppose q < (1 - epsilon) omega. Then (1 + gamma) q < (1 + gamma)(1 - epsilon) omega, hence
     omega < (1 + gamma)(1 - epsilon) omega + gamma
           = (1 - epsilon) omega + gamma (1 + omega) - gamma epsilon omega
           = (1 - epsilon) omega + epsilon omega - gamma epsilon omega
           = omega - gamma epsilon omega.
     This is impossible, since gamma epsilon omega > 0.
   (v) Therefore q >= (1 - epsilon) omega, i.e. M(s) = q s^n >= (1 - epsilon) omega s^n.
   (vi) As s < r < 2r, step 1 gives mu(B_s(y)) = ofReal(M(s)) >= ofReal((1 - epsilon)(omega s^n)), by monotonicity of ofReal.

7. Conclusion. By steps 5 and 6, for every epsilon > 0 the inequality ofReal((1 - epsilon)(omega s^n)) <= mu(B_s(y)) holds for all s in a right-neighbourhood of 0, i.e. eventually along s -> 0+ (the filter 𝓝[>] 0).

Remark (use in the parent; not part of the proof). Then mu(B_(2r)(y)) < infinity because B_(2r)(y) is a compact subset of B_rho(0) ⊆ U, and the a.e. estimate is supplied by ted_dge1_density_le_monotone_bound, ted_lp_monotonicity and ted_tangent_plane_facts (3) together with theta >= 1 mu-a.e.
